📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh).

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

According to recent reports, the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

The Best Gifts for Overlanders Who Love to Explore Off-Road

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life.
  • Tires are the most crucial overland upgrade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life. Fear not. As an overlander myself, I’ve compiled a comprehensive gift list that has suggestions for overland rookies and veterans alike. I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so major they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most crucial overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

It has been revealed that overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Recent findings suggest that airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

In a recent development, folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Sources indicate that coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

It has been revealed that the REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I can connect solar panels to add juice at camp, or I can wire it to my alternator so it gets topped off while I’m driving. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

It has been revealed that iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Recent findings suggest that two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.

Overlanding requires a lot of gear. The best way to keep it all organized is a Kitworks Gear Box. Infinitely customizable, the Gear Box is the perfect storage method for a camp kitchen, recovery gear, dry food, even clothing. Made from honeycomb panels covered in a 900-denier ripstop shell, the box has proven just as durable as any hard-sided competitor.

Don’t invest in a dash-mounted radio—get two of these instead. With an ultra-reliable, multi-day battery and huge range, these radios are the best way to stay in touch with buddies when cell phones don’t work. When I’m not using the radios in my truck, I use them to keep in contact while backcountry skiing, hunting, and other off-grid adventures.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

The Gozney Arc XL pizza oven makes outdoor entertaining easy year-round, from backyard pizza parties to après-ski gatherings. (Photo: Courtesy of Gozney).

I wrote about my Gozney Arc XL pizza oven two summers ago, when it became the pie de resistance for using my backyard to get outside more (and for a suspicious number of new friends showing up at my house). More than a year later, I’m happy to report that the novelty hasn’t worn off. If anything, I love it more.

One of my favorite ways to spend a Sunday afternoon, or unwind after a mountain bike ride, is inviting friends over for homemade pizzas. Everyone brings their favorite toppings, we experiment with different combinations, and dinner becomes an activity in itself. It’s dinner and a show, and everyone gets fed. And because we keep ours on a covered porch with adequate ventilation, pizza night doesn’t end when winter arrives. Après-ski pizza parties might actually be my favorite use for it.

The Gozney Arc XL makes it ridiculously easy. It runs on propane (I use the same tank from my grill), reaches temperatures up to 950°F, and can cook a 16-inch pizza in as little as 60 seconds. Its lateral rolling flame distributes heat across the oven, so you don’t have to constantly rotate your pizza. The result is that perfectly blistered, chewy crust I usually associate with my favorite wood-fired pizza joints now in my own backyard.

It has been revealed that gozney makes several ovens, from more portable models to larger, more elaborate setups (many are also on sale right now). The Arc XL hits the sweet spot for me because it’s compact enough for our back patio, still with plenty of room to maneuver a full-size pizza.

Recent findings suggest that you can make your own dough, buy Gozney’s mixes, or do what we do: keep Trader Joe’s premade pizza dough in the freezer so we’re always ready for an impromptu pizza night. One tip: a little semolina flour on your pizza peel helps the dough slide into the oven without sticking.

Sources indicate that my favorite toppings? Peaches, burrata, prosciutto, basil, and hot honey. Comment yours!

Recent findings suggest that learn from my mistake. When I first bought my Arc XL, I skipped the matching stand for a cheaper rolling cart from Amazon. It was a nightmare to assemble, felt flimsy, and looked terrible. I recently upgraded to the actual Gozney stand, and the difference is night and day. It’s sturdy, streamlined, easy to move, and designed to hold the oven securely. I should have trusted Gozney from the start.

It has been revealed that the stand has a 4.8-out-of-5-star rating from 204 customer reviews, so apparently plenty of people knew something I didn’t. Worth the upgrade, especially while it’s on sale.

If you’re shopping for someone who already owns a Gozney, the brand’s pizza peels, dough trays, and other accessories make excellent gifts and are also on sale for Black Friday.

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In a recent development, in the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Industry observers note that later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a latest route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Sources indicate that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management proposal for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

Recent findings suggest that “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher noted. Although that initial proposal was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

Industry observers note that as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular significant wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions mentioned.

    #147894. She Asked the Appalachian Trail Conservancy to Start an Artist Residency. Now You Can Apply, Too.

    She Asked the Appalachian Trail Conservancy to Start an Artist Residency. Now You Can Apply, Too.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that when Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem.
    • Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting.
    • In a recent development, from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that when Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem. They didn’t have one.

    So she sent a cold email. Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting. It was perfect timing: The ATC was approaching its centennial in 2025 and looking for new ways to get more hikers on trail. As Caroline Ralston, the ATC’s associate vice president of marketing and communications, put it, “at that time, we realized we didn’t really have anything for creatives.”.

    In a recent development, from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield. She’d already put in miles on the John Muir Trail (JMT), the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), and the Tahoe Rim Trail, and was starting to see a clearer connection between her creative life and her hiking.

    A 454-mile stretch of the PCT found its way into 30 titanium brooches shaped like lengths of paracord. Their colors and patterns changed with her mood on the trail, day by day. Her stories became a zine. So when she and Jackson started talking through possible structures for the ATC’s inaugural artist in residence program, she offered herself up as the guinea pig.

    It has been revealed that last year, when the Conservancy officially debuted the program, Weston set out from Georgia as its pilot creative. “Almost a year after I planted the seed for this wild idea, somehow, things came together to make it a reality,” Weston wrote in her blog.

    Industry observers note that since metalwork is specialized and far from portable, she used the hike as an inspiration gathering exercise rather than a time to actually create work. She couldn’t haul a forge, but she could carry a camera. Back in Philadelphia, she’s been picking through her thousands of photographs, taking another look at the pile of butterfly wings she came across, or the blazes she passed.

    According to recent reports, “Hiking the trail as the ATC’s Artist in Residence has motivated me to be more observant of my surroundings,” Weston told the ATC. “I’ve been actively documenting the experience through photography and journaling, wanting to remember the rich details of my hike and use them to generate artwork from the vivid text and images I’ve collected.”.

    Weston had one piece finished before she ever set foot on the AT. For the trail’s centennial, she designed an enamel pin that hikers could pick up at a visitor center.

    Recent findings suggest that the ATC is now looking for its 2027 Artist in Residence, and artists working in any medium have until January 3, 2027, to apply. The residency includes a limited stipend for transportation and lodging for events along the AT, and a two- to four-week stay at Maine’s Monson Arts, an arts center in the last town NOBO hikers pass through before the 100-Mile wilderness. Weston spent five months walking the entire AT, but the next resident could hike a section or spend their time in one town along the trail; the residency’s structure is malleable.

    Recent findings suggest that “This program is a fresh way to experience the trail,” claims Ralston. “When the trail was first conceptualized over 100 years ago, one of the founding ideas was that people need a place to escape, connect with nature, and unplug. This program is an extension of that. We want to invite artists to immerse themselves on the trail, connect with nature, and see what kind of inspiration comes from it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that along with a résumé or CV and five to 10 work samples, applicants must provide an artist statement and a work proposal. The ATC wants to know what you make, what time on the trail might bring to your work, and how you’d share it.

    What makes an application stand out? For Ralston, notable applications will express “a desire to get out there, and a desire to share it publicly.” For Weston, that meant giving talks at trail centers.

    In a recent development, her advice to the next applicant? Think about what a stretch of time on this particular trail might change about the work you already do, and leave yourself some room to be surprised. For Weston, one of those surprises came in her first week out of Georgia.

    The first time Weston spotted pink lady’s slipper orchids on the AT, her husband was hiking with her. He’d come along for the first stretch and they saw a few patches together that week. Each flower had a little pouch that she found “kind of weird and grotesque looking, but also very beautiful.” By the time she came across a whole field of them, her husband had gone home to Philadelphia. “I’m all alone, and here’s all these orchids,” she remembers thinking.

    It has been revealed that now, back in her Philadelphia studio, she’s working on a recreation of a pink lady’s slipper. Of all the things she saw in five months on trail, that one made what she calls a “one to one translation” into her work.

    “Now that I’m back in Philadelphia, I’m distilling all of that experience into work that emerges from it,” states Weston.

    #147893. After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (975 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025.
    • On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable declared his initiative to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.
    • “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025. The wildfire burned more than 145,000 acres and destroyed 114 structures, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge (Photo: slovegrove/Getty).

    On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable declared his initiative to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

    “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU. In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

    Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

    The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management plans and communication logs.

    Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

    “I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

    Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

    Sources indicate that A career government attorney, Keable spent 23 years in the Interior Department’s Office of the Solicitor, including eight years as assistant solicitor of general law, before his appointment in April 2020 during President Donald Trump’s first administration. He had no previous experience working for the National Park Service.

    The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an organization representing current and former park service employees, issued a statement on April 3, 2020, criticizing Keable’s selection the same day the NPS declared his appointment.

    “Ed Keable is not qualified to manage and lead a complicated park such as the Grand Canyon,” Phil Francis, then-chair of the coalition, stated in the statement.

    In the appointment announcement, NPS Deputy Director David Vela praised Keable’s leadership abilities and cited his experience within the Interior Department as an asset to the park.

    Sources indicate that sparked by lightning on July 4, 2025, the Dragon Bravo Fire burned more than 145,000 acres over nearly three months and cost an estimated $141 million to suppress, according to the federal report. Investigators concluded that “the most consequential drivers were not environmental,” finding that many of the challenges the NPS and firefighters encountered during the blaze were “foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues.”.

    In the report, investigators determined that “leadership roles did not align with expertise or decision making authority.” As the fire’s agency administrator, Keable was responsible for overseeing firefighting strategy and authorizing suppression tactics.

    According to recent reports, under NPS guidelines, superintendents at wildfire-prone parks are expected to qualify for that role within two years of their appointment. Five years into his tenure, Keable still lacked that qualification, the report remarked. Although qualified administrators were available locally, the park didn’t bring one in until July 30, nearly four weeks after the fire ignited.

    In a recent development, keable initially approved a strategy known as confine and contain, which involves keeping a wildfire within designated boundaries rather than extinguishing it entirely. The approach conflicted with 2025 federal guidance against managing wildfires for ecological benefit, though investigators indicated that Keable had not received that, the report said.

    Park leadership reaffirmed the strategy twice over the next five days, during which the fire breached planned containment lines.

    “Continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk,” investigators wrote.

    Communication failures also delayed firefighters’ efforts to slow the blaze using aerial fire retardant. Keable authorized retardant drops on July 13, once an earlier request from firefighters was clarified, but by then, the Grand Canyon Lodge had already burned.

    The report stopped short of assigning individual fault. “The Dragon Bravo Fire should be understood as a warning event,” the report stated. “The findings demonstrate outcomes were shaped less by tactical execution than by NPS systemic complications related to authority, qualifications, and decision processes.”.

    As Outside reported in April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested that full suppression might have prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in property losses, though wildland firefighters noted that the canyon’s steep terrain initially made ground operations unsafe.

    The National Park Service advertised Keable’s position on November 24, with applications closing December 8 and an annual salary ranging from $162,740 to $228,000. Responsibilities include overseeing wildland firefighting, emergency medical services, and backcountry rescues.

    It has been revealed that the job hunt comes at a pressing time for the national park. A devastating flash flood on August 29 destroyed trails and infrastructure along the Colorado River and led to three deaths. Facilities on the South Rim went without running water for nearly two months until the park restored water service to six lodges on November 20.

    Among the next superintendent’s biggest challenges will be rebuilding the North Rim. Earlier this month, the park service concluded a public comment period on three preliminary redevelopment concepts for the area. Congress is also considering the North Rim Restoration Act, which would give the park service greater contracting flexibility to expedite reconstruction.

    In a recent development, sections of the fire-damaged North Rim reopened to visitors in May, but the August flash flood hindered reconstruction efforts, washing out trails and damaging bridges and critical infrastructure. The entire North Kaibab Trail and Cottonwood Campground remain closed, and Phantom Ranch’s lodging closure has been extended through January 31, 2027.

    #147892. Latest Update: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2375 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
    • My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
    • Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

    My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

    Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

    According to recent reports, I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

    According to recent reports, on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

    Recent findings suggest that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

    Industry observers note that packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

    According to recent reports, hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

    Sources indicate that I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

    In a recent development, as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

    Recent findings suggest that the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

    It has been revealed that as excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

    I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

    It has been revealed that at that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

    Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

    According to recent reports, alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

    Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

    It has been revealed that I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

    Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

    According to recent reports, the climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

    The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

    Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

    It has been revealed that when we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

    In a recent development, at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

    It has been revealed that alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

    Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

    Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

    Sources indicate that some ultralight thru-hikers swear by going stoveless to save weight and time. But when you don’t cook, you might assume there are a few other things you have to do without: full flavor, fresh ingredients, and a diverse slate of nutrients, to name a few. Cold soaking—the popular method of rehydrating dry or instant food with cold water—lets you ditch the stove, fuel canister, and cook pot. But does it also have to mean compromising on a satisfying meal?

    Not necessarily. Going stoveless doesn’t have to be all cold couscous, stale chips, and stray sauce packets. Wild Planet offers ready-to-eat wild tuna bowls that are packed with protein and full of flavor. Featuring wild-caught skipjack tuna and organic ingredients, they’re a nutritious solution for anyone looking to fuel up without the fuel canister.

    For the no-cook-curious, Wild Planet’s meals make for an easy transition from stove-cooked, pre-packaged backpacking meals, saving ounces while offering similar—or better—nutritional value and flavor.

    Take the Wild Tuna and Red Bean Bowl, for example. It’s a tasty combination of skipjack tuna, organic beans, sweetcorn, red peppers, carrots, and spices in organic extra virgin olive oil. It offers 290 calories, with 18 grams of protein, 5 grams of fiber, and 100 milligrams of DHA omega-3s per package/serving. Each peel-and-eat package is one serving and weighs only 5.6 ounces.

    It’s similar to other popular backpacking meals in both weight and nutrients per serving. But Wild Planet’s meals are ready to eat in seconds, no cooking or cold soaking required. In fact, you can bring four Wild Planet meals and still carry less than the weight of just one competing meal when combined with the weight of a typical lightweight stove, pot, and fuel. With all that weight savings, you can still add any crunchy toppings, sauces, and cheeses to boost your calorie count on major days. It’s an easy trail lunch that doesn’t compromise when it comes to flavor or nutrition.

    Industry observers note that it’s the combination of real, thoughtfully selected ingredients and no-prep convenience that sets Wild Planet’s meals apart. A lot of hikers go stoveless and resort to the bare essentials—“soaked quinoa plus whatever is on hand.” You can do better. When you hike with a Wild Tuna and Quinoa Bowl, you’ve got ingredients that are caught, grown, and chosen with intention. That means wild skipjack tuna, organic quinoa, delicious veggies, and gourmet spices, all sealed in organic extra virgin olive oil.

    Hikers are naturally innovative, and with some thought, cold-soaking can deliver surprisingly elevated meals. If you want to try it for yourself, or want tips to supplement your ready-to-eat meals, here are a few basics:.

    It has been revealed that real ingredients are always a delicious luxury in the backcountry, even for the savviest of chefs. It’s one of the appeals of Wild Planet’s tuna bowls, especially for those upcoming to stoveless backpacking. You can just pack and peel, then pair your summit views with wild-caught tuna, whole foods, and carefully crafted flavors.

    Sources indicate that as a hiker, you know the importance of low-impact practices. Wild Planet believes the same. The brand prioritizes sustainable fishing practices and ocean health, and uses only pole-and-line and troll fishing methods to catch its tuna. That means hauling in only one fish per line at a time; this selective fishing has benefits for the ocean and for you.

    In a recent development, on the environmental side, these sustainable methods are focused on preventing two of the most damaging effects of the commercial fishing industry on ocean ecosystems—overfishing and bycatch. Overfishing depletes a fish population faster than it has the chance to repopulate. Bycatch, meanwhile, occurs when non-targeted species are hauled in by accident, like sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Wild Planet’s select fishing partners don’t use nets; they monitor closely for bycatch while reeling in one fish at a time.

    #147889. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1342 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
    • Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Fresh York near the Gunks.
    • Industry observers note that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good tech giant.”.

    Sources indicate that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Fresh York near the Gunks. Currently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she states of her big three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

    Industry observers note that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

    It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

    It has been revealed that I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

    When Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

    Sources indicate that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

    We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

    First, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

    Industry observers note that very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

    Industry observers note that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

    According to recent reports, then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

    In a recent development, so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

    According to recent reports, will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

    Every time we got to a newly introduced belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

    According to recent reports, none of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

    At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he said it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never revealed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

    Recent findings suggest that we got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

    Industry observers note that I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

    Sources indicate that it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a major light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

    To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

    Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Fresh York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

    In a recent development, as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

    According to recent reports, got your own tale of getting benighted? Submit it here.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Better for the Sea, Better for You

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals.
    • Thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems.
    • It has been revealed that according to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals. And it’s not just for hikers and campers. Canned and pouched seafood has been steadily rising in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and convenience. But while tuna can be a great choice for your health, how do you know if it’s a good choice for the environment?

    Thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems. Here’s why it matters.

    It has been revealed that according to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States. That means a lot of tuna harvested from the world’s oceans, making harmful fishing practices even more harmful due to the enormity of the scale. This puts tuna and other fish populations at risk, and unfortunately, these practices still dominate the industry.

    In a recent development, purse seine fishing, which is responsible for about 66% of global tropical tuna catch, per the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation, can be harmful, especially when used in conjunction with fish aggregating devices (FADs). This method involves using a large wall of netting—up to 6,500 feet long and reaching around 650 feet in depth—to surround an entire school of fish. Non-selective mass fishing practices can deplete a population before it has a chance to properly reproduce, especially since it indiscriminately removes juvenile tuna from the ecosystem, threatening healthy repopulation.

    Another key threat from large-scale industrial fishing is bycatch, or the unintentional harvesting of non-targeted species. Some of the species most impacted by the tuna industry include sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Net-based fishing with FADs is the most common culprit, since FADs don’t discriminate between which types of fish they attract. Bycatch also frequently occurs with longline fishing, which uses baited lines an average of 28 miles long. Animals caught as bycatch often do not survive.

    How can things be done differently? Wild Planet is a case study. Since 2004, Wild Planet has focused on sourcing seafood through responsible fishing practices. Its wild albacore and skipjack tuna showcase how responsible fishing and high-quality products can—and should—go hand in hand.

    All of Wild Planet’s tuna are caught individually using pole-and-line or trolling methods. Pole-and-line is exactly what it sounds like: one pole, one line, and one fish at a time. Trolling is similar, with multiple lines towed behind a slow-moving boat. Both the bait used and the speed at which the boat travels are specifically chosen to attract the targeted species. In both methods, fish are hauled in immediately, so non-targeted species can be quickly released.

    The benefits of these inherently selective methods are twofold. First, they allow Wild Planet to specifically target tuna while minimizing bycatch of other marine species. Additionally, the company’s responsible fishing operations are able to further select what kind of tuna is being harvested. Wild Planet sources younger migratory tuna near the ocean’s surface, avoiding juvenile fish, who are key to repopulation efforts, and older, larger tuna that tend to accumulate higher levels of mercury. It’s an approach that’s better for you and the planet.

    The Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch Program has a name for foods like this: Super Greens. It’s an exclusive list—it right now includes only 10 foods—that points to pole-and-line caught tuna as an option that’s high in omega-3s, low in mercury, and harvested with the ocean in mind.

    The Monterey Bay Aquarium has a unique relationship with Wild Planet. The brand has not only been following the aquarium’s guidance since the beginning, but the institution is actually key to the company’s origin story. It was at a Monterey Bay Aquarium exhibit on fragile ocean ecosystems that Wild Planet founder Bill Carvalho was inspired to build a different kind of seafood company.

    It has been revealed that the Aquarium, in turn, is inspired by the efforts that many in the industry have taken in response to its suggestions. “Some of these companies have been with us from the very beginning,” Shawn Cronin, market engagement director for Seafood Watch stated in 2024. “They make it easy for people to choose responsible seafood day-to-day, helping move the needle through their sourcing and by directly engaging in global improvement initiatives. It’s not an easy commitment to make.”.

    It has been revealed that that emphasis on doing what’s right and trusting the science continues today. It’s the kind of thinking that guides the way Wild Planet fishes as well as the types of fish it sells. In addition to tuna, Wild Planet also sells mackerel, anchovies, and sardines. These smaller, lower-food-chain species can be more abundant and offer another responsibly sourced seafood option, while delivering plenty of protein, omega-3s, and flavor.

    Industry observers note that if you’re looking to incorporate more sustainable seafood into your life, the same principles extend beyond tuna. Always look for labels that call out pole-and-line caught, troll caught, and/or FAD-free fishing. Other information, like the specific species and where it was harvested, lets you know that the company knows—and cares—where its fish come from.

    In a recent development, you can find out what sustainability tastes like for yourself. From now until December 22, Outside readers get 20% off everything on Wild Planet’s website with code OUTSIDE20. Because even though the impact of our choices might be harder to see when it’s an ocean away, it’s no less notable.

    In a recent development, founded in 2004, Wild Planet is the first large-scale sustainably focused canned seafood tech giant in the U.S. Committed to protecting marine ecosystems for future generations, Wild Planet sources 100% wild-caught seafood using the highest sustainability standards, delivering nutrient-dense, minimally processed products that are as close to nature as possible. Learn more at WildPlanetFoods.com.

    #147884. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

    A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).
    • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.
    • The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

    A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

    The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

    “On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

    It has been revealed that AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

    Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

    Located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

    Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

    Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

    “If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard noted. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

    Sources indicate that batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

    Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

    In a recent development, similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

    Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard stated he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

    Sources indicate that “They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard mentioned. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. After rapidly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

    According to recent reports, after quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

    • Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) stated in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A helicopter transports a deceased hiker recovered from Humboldt Peak. (Photo: Custer County Sheriff's Office).

    A hiker who went missing on a Colorado 14er earlier this week was found dead from an apparent fall on November 24, following a three-day search that sent rescuers combing the high country in winter conditions.

    Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) stated in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.

    It has been revealed that authorities mentioned that the hiker had summited 14,068-foot Humboldt Peak solo early on the morning of Sunday, November 22. At 5 p.m., CCSAR was notified that the hiker still hadn’t returned, and sent teams into the field alongside aerial support from Reach Air and Flight for Life. The missing hiker had shared his proposal with his family; however, while rescuers quickly located his car, they were unable to locate him despite searching through the night in winter weather. Additional ground teams joined the search the following morning, but fared no better.

    In a recent development, after pausing the search for the night, 21 volunteers, including K9 teams and drone operators, returned to the field on Tuesday. During the operation, authorities closed the South Colony area to cars and hikers.

    In a statement, the Custer County Sheriff’s Office offered its condolences to the deceased hiker’s family, friends, and fiancé, and stated that both the hiker’s strategy and cell phone forensics helped authorities determine where they should look.

    Industry observers note that compared to other 14ers in the same area, the hike up Humboldt is relatively straightforward. The standard West Ridge route follows the feature of the same name roughly 11 miles out and back to the summit. During fall and winter, however, snow and ice can both make it more difficult to stay on-route and increase the consequences of a slip on the peak’s exposed ridgeline. It was not immediately clear which route the hiker took to the summit.

    The nearby South Colony SNOTEL station, which sits at 10,800 feet, recorded 16 inches of snow on the ground on November 22, up nearly 7 inches from the week prior.

Today’s jackets use the latest advances in insulation and waterproofing to replace two or three traditional layers, and adapt better to changing conditions and activity levels.

We tested these jackets in conditions ranging from wind-blown fall rain to frigid cold mountain mornings, and they consistently kept us moving forward with minimal fuss, wrapped in warmth and shielded from the elements.

    Pros and Cons + Surprisingly warm + Unrestrictive fit + Smart vent panels – No hood.

    Sources indicate that the Thermalrunner proved an excellent choice for a surprisingly broad range of temperatures and weather conditions. On a blustery 40-degree day with light rain, the water-resistant fabric treatment handled the challenge, beading moisture on the exterior while the soft interior lining stayed dry against the skin. On another run when the sun burned through clouds unexpectedly fast, we were impressed by how well the vent panels in the back shed excess heat. One tester called the lightweight PrimalLoft insulation a “Goldilocks” amount of warmth that consistently tamed the chill without overheating him.

    Pros and Cons + Featherweight + Packable + Protective hood – Fragile.

    Stuffing the Aerolight Wind Jacket into a pack before heading out on an adventurous mountain trek in the Swiss Alps proved to be a good decision for one tester. Late in the afternoon, the summer skies filled with clouds, the temperature dropped, and bursts of rain started soaking the mountainside. The jacket provided immediate warmth, blocked the wind, and, though it’s by no means waterproof, kept enough moisture out to keep moving comfortably—with almost no weight penalty.

    The water-resistant treatment is PFAS-free, and small touches like an adjustable hood and elastic wrist cuffs add to the better-than-expected protection. The ultralight fabric is soft and quiet on the move and breathes well at high exertion levels, but offers no stretch. The lone chest pocket doubles as a stuff sack, making this a great item to keep on hand for mild days in the 40s and 50s. The feather-weight construction comes at the price of being somewhat more fragile than other top picks: we’ve heard reports of the fabric blowing out under stress, although we didn’t see any excess wear during testing.

    Pros and Cons + Windproof + Highly visible + Distinctive look – Lacks breathability.

    When was the last time someone on the street complimented your running outfit for looking good? Our testers got compliments on the PYNRS (pronounced like “pioners”) Magnolia Track Jacket all the time. This NYC-based company started as an inclusive urban running club before branching into apparel; the result is functional outerwear that stands out from the crowd.

    Industry observers note that the iridescent, tightly woven nylon shell features reflective piping for excellent visibility from all sides, and the polyester lining is soft against skin. Cut on the looser side, this jacket easily accommodated insulating layers and proved comfortable for running in near- and sub-freezing weather. It offers roomy, zippered hand pockets and an interior zippered chest pocket, plus elasticized cuffs and a drawstring waist to seal out the weather. The jacket is a little hefty and lacks some of the breathability higher-performance materials offer, but for cool-to-cold weather running (low 40s to mid-20s), we stayed comfortably warm and looked stylish in the Magnolia Track Jacket.

    Start ready and stay ready with this do-anything hooded workout layer. Crafted from a soft performance stretch knit, this jacket is both insulating and flexible with a protective woven overlay that gives you added coverage in cool and variable conditions. It wicks moisture and includes a drawcord hood and zip pockets to keep you and your belongings dry and safe in any weather. Pair it with the Vuori Sunday bottoms to make the perfect set.

    Pros and Cons + Soft wool fabric + Polartec insulation + Wind-blocking torso – No reflectivity.

    The Alpha Active’s medium-weight blend of Merino wool and polyester, with a touch of bamboo rayon, proved exceptionally soft and warm, and excelled at wicking moisture away from skin. Baffled Polartec Alpha insulation and a wind-blocking nylon fabric overlay the chest. The overall effect felt like wearing a lightweight vest over a premium base-layer shirt—but integrated into a single piece that moved comfortably and quietly with us.

    Industry observers note that the breathable Merino-blend sleeves and back, with no wind-blocking material, kept us from overheating at easier paces up to the 50-degree mark. The jacket proved comfortable down to freezing when working hard—adding a lightweight outer shell produced a warm combination that handled all but the most bitter or windy conditions. The sleek fit and black fabric look good, but bring a reflective hat or wear a light for nighttime running.

    Pros and Cons + Toasty, 95% recycled fleece front + Functional and stylish fit + Solid warmth – No backside windblock.

    Recent findings suggest that our testers agreed that the front of this attractive jacket provided solid insulation for frigid conditions. They were divided, however, on whether it would have benefited from better wind-blocking on the back, where a large fabric panel vented heat, leaving some feeling too exposed to the elements. Still, at an affordable price, most reviewers found the Winter Warm Pro kept them comfortable in temperatures well below freezing (there’s no hood, so bring a hat for frigid days). The body fabric fleece is made with 95 percent recycled materials, feels soft against bare skin, and stretches nicely. The polyester torso insulation is reassuringly thick without feeling bulky. Additional touches include a water-repellent coating, hand pockets, side mesh storage pocket, and a zippered chest pocket.

    Pros and Cons + Stormproof + Effective hood and brim + Chest snap – Crinkly.

    It has been revealed that salomon’s adv.DRY material—a thin, microporous membrane bonded to a nylon shell—proved impressively waterproof during drenching rain showers while staying breathable in dry conditions. The Bonatti Pro features fully taped seams, waterproof zippers, and an excellent, adjustable brimmed hood that kept our hair dry and our heads warm without impeding our field of vision, even on the move. A snap closure at the chest lets you open the zipper and vent heat promptly without removing the jacket, and reflective patches on the front and back provide good visibility in poor weather.

    Recent findings suggest that the fit is close yet roomy enough to accommodate insulating underlayers, extending the jacket’s comfortable range below the freezing mark. The fabric is somewhat crinkly, but it still packs easily into a small bundle. There are vents at the waist, but they’re fairly minimal, and we didn’t notice much airflow. Salomon’s “aeroPACK” flap system is meant to accommodate a small hydration backpack without impeding the jacket’s fit; we didn’t test this feature but noted that it didn’t get in the way when running without a pack.

    Choosing the best winter running jacket is primarily about the kinds of winter conditions you face where you live, travel, and run. Consider if you need a waterproof layer, or can get by with water resistance—waterproof jackets are more costly, don’t breathe as well, and tend to be somewhat stiffer and noisier, but are worth it when you’re out in a downpour or blizzard.

    Then think about whether you want your running jacket to be insulated and provide warmth on its own, or work as a thin, exterior shell layer. Insulated jackets can make heading out in frigid temps less daunting, especially if you tend to run cold, but can get hot during high-intensity exercise or if the temps rise. Shell jackets allow you to layer underneath to adjust for a range of conditions. Also consider whether you want a fitted jacket that stays close to the body for streamlined mobility, or a looser fit that allows flexibility for layering underneath.

    The jacket review test crew put these products through their paces in locations as diverse as the Swiss Alps and Nebraska’s High Plains, logging miles on both roads and trails. Testers recorded their notes for each sample piece during easy runs, up-tempo workouts, and everything in between, in good weather and full-on storm conditions. Jackets were evaluated for their effectiveness at keeping testers warm and blocking wind and moisture while breathing and venting excess heat, with bonus points given for the versatility to handle a range of weather conditions and to look good in diverse contexts.

    Recent findings suggest that lead reviewer Mark Eller is based in Boulder, Colorado. He’s logged three Boston Marathons, completed trail-running ultras, and has raced in multiple off-road and on-road triathlons. He also enjoys snowboarding and Nordic skiing on Colorado’s Front Range and central mountains, and he frequently rows a single scull at the Boulder Reservoir.

    Brian Metzler is a freelance writer and the founding editor of Trail Runner. A former walk-on Division I track athlete, he mostly runs on mountainous trails nowadays in Boulder and Leadville, Colorado.

    Kurt Actenhagen enjoys trail running, mountain biking, and exploring mountain ranges from the High Sierra to Colorado’s most remote peaks. He’s set Fastest Known Times and achieved ultra-distance milestones, but he also enjoys a leisurely hike.Jonathan Beverly is no stranger to winter weather. He began running in high school on the Maine coast, trained for marathons for years in Upcoming York, and now can be found chasing windmills in the western Nebraska Sandhills, accompanied by his two dogs. He is the senior running gear editor for Outside.
