    #147879. What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1566 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the author climbing in Substantial Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah.
    • Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting.
    • Have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the author climbing in Substantial Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

    Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

    Have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

    Intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

    Sources indicate that while no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a upcoming book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

    “We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson states.

    After giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

    A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

    Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

    Most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

    Recent findings suggest that some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

    Industry observers note that others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber noted they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

    It has been revealed that with all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson says. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

    “While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson says.

    So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

    In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

    In a recent development, most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

    Sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

    Recent findings suggest that “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

    If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

    It has been revealed that then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

    Next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

    It has been revealed that most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson indicates it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

    An important thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

    What if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson states to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

    Industry observers note that since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

    It has been revealed that with distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

    In the case of eustress, Robertson says you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

    It has been revealed that to seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson notes. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

    It has been revealed that parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.

    #147877. Latest Update: You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: You’ve Heard “Be Bold, Start Cold.” But How Cold is Too Cold?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning.
    • According to recent reports, but how cold is too cold?
    • When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Alex Ratson/Getty Images).

    In a recent development, hike long enough and you’ll inevitably hear the phrase, “Be Bold, Start Cold.” It’s catchy, easy to remember and generally good advice for anyone starting out early in the morning. On its surface, it’s simple: Don’t bother wearing a ton of layers you’ll take off the first fifteen minutes into your walk. Starting a little colder means skipping the first half mile shed and letting your body naturally warm up to its resting active temperature.

    According to recent reports, but how cold is too cold? How do you tell the difference between a chill that’ll wear off by the first switchback and a sign you should’ve kept your jacket on? Does the first fifteen minutes warming up do more harm than good?

    When I asked Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth, about the old mountaineering phrase, he generally agreed with the principal but thought it needed a bit more nuance.

    Tipton has spent four decades studying how the body regulates its temperature, and part of his research looks at what happens to hands and feet during prolonged exposure to cold. His studies have informed the British Royal Navy’s approach to cooling overheated officers, and he’s worked with the U.S. Coast Guard to develop a model that estimates how long someone lost at sea might survive in cold water.

    His advice for hikers was simple: have a smart layering strategy. He didn’t take glitch with “Be Bold,” but thought hikers should take more care when it comes to starting cold.

    It has been revealed that so how do you tell whether you’re underdressed or overprepared? We talked to Tipton, Appalachian Mountain Club guide Marielle Fibish, and western North Carolina search and rescue team member Nancy East about what to wear for the first mile of a winter hike, how to tell when it’s time to add or shed a layer, and when you’re better off starting warm.

    In a recent development, for East, a good starting point is how you feel while you’re waiting for a hiking partner to lace up their boots. Can you stand around comfortably for a few minutes? “It’s the type of chill that fresh clothes from the dryer would immediately quell,” she says.

    Tipton suggests paying attention to your hands. As your body cools, blood flow to your fingers decreases, which can make something as simple as working a zipper harder. In his view, “the ideal place to be is where your extremities feel warm, but you’re not producing vast amounts of sweat.”.

    Once you’re walking, pay attention to which way things are headed. Is that slight chill wearing off, or are your fingers getting colder with every switchback?

    “If my hands are getting cold, I’m shivering, or I’m not generating enough body heat to feel comfortable after several minutes of hiking, I’ll add a layer,” East states.

    Recent findings suggest that when Fibish gets dressed for a winter hike in the White Mountains, she checks the forecast, then dresses as though it’s about 10°F warmer. Say it’s 20°F at the trailhead. Fibish dresses the way she would for a walk in 30°F weather. The puffy, shell, and extra mittens are all coming with her. They just get to ride in her bag for the first mile.

    One mistake Fibish sees is hikers reaching for the same outfit they’d wear to the ski hill.

    “Insulated snow pants and jackets are great for downhill skiing and making snowmen, but they can be too warm for other outdoor winter activities like hiking or Nordic skiing,” she indicates. For hiking, she builds her outfit around a close-fitting wool top and bottoms, with hiking or soft-shell pants over the base layer. A separate fleece gives her some warmth she can shed on the first climb without losing her protection from the wind.

    Fibish also thinks about who’s coming along. If you’re breaking trail for the group, you might be glad you left your fleece in your pack. If you tend to run cold and expect to spend some of that first mile waiting for friends, you might want to keep it on. Give yourself five or ten minutes of walking, Fibish notes, and you’ll have a better sense of how well you guessed.

    Recent findings suggest that for Fibish, the first cue to lose a layer is a little tingle of warmth building under her clothes. Sometimes slipping off her hat or hiking in glove liners is enough. On a sustained climb, she might stop to take off her fleece. As Tipton explains, your working muscles produce heat. Taking off a layer lets more of that heat escape into the air, so your body can regulate its core temperature with less sweating.

    Your hands can tell you when it’s time to add a layer, too. As your body cools, Tipton explains, blood vessels near the skin narrow to conserve heat in your core. That leaves less warm blood flowing to your fingers. East pays attention when her hands start getting colder, even if she’s still walking. She’ll also pull on a layer if she starts to shiver or if several minutes of hiking haven’t warmed her up. “I don’t wait until I’m genuinely cold to do something about it,” she says.

    A snack break is one layer change you can see coming. Once you stop climbing, your muscles produce less heat, but sweat evaporating from your damp shirt keeps cooling you. If the wind picks up at the top, East pulls on a fleece or puffy, followed by a windproof layer, before she settles in to eat. Jacket first, sandwich second.

    East likes to know what those first ten minutes of walking are going to look like. If it’s especially cold, wet, or windy, she’ll start a little warmer. Same goes for an exposed stretch of trail: If the climb starts somewhere on the other side of a windy meadow, you’ve still got the meadow to cross. You can take your jacket off when you get into an area with more coverage.

    So is “be bold, start cold” good advice? If you’re about to head uphill and you know you’ll be peeling off your fleece by the first switchback, sure. If you’re already cold standing there, you can keep it on and blueprint to stop a few minutes up the trail.

    It has been revealed that on early starts in the Himalayas, Tipton’s group would stop five minutes up the trail so everyone could adjust their layers. It’s advice worth taking. Pick a spot a few minutes up the trail while everyone’s still gearing up. That way, nobody has to be the first to ask, “Mind if I stop and take this thing off?”.

    East has her own version of the phrase: “Start cool, but don’t stay cold.”.

    #147876. The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Fresh Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1707 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Fresh Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
    • According to recent reports, the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
    • In a recent development, moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

    According to recent reports, the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

    In a recent development, moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

    It has been revealed that chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The new rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

    The charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

    Adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

    “As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” says Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

    “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain owners, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” states Rodrigues. “That remarked, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

    According to recent reports, the charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

    In a recent development, “This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

    Industry observers note that I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential newly introduced rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

    According to recent reports, the TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

    In a recent development, under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

    The charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” notes Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

    Nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret says the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

    The variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” states Perret.

    Industry observers note that “The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she notes, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you swiftly and swiftly out of it.”.

    Day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he claims. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

    Sources indicate that multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the organization Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

    I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any concern. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

    One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

    It has been revealed that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the big monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

    #147875. Industry News: A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

    Industry News: A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
    • Sources indicate that in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
    • Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

    Sources indicate that in 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

    Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

    “To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

    That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) released a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

    “People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett said.

    Sources indicate that as part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

    Industry observers note that “You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett mentioned. “Just take pictures.”.

    Nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility problems, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett indicates enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

    “For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett remarked.

    Industry observers note that kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people blueprint their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

    Industry observers note that “We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

    The map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that reveals the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

    Industry observers note that the tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as Upcoming Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

    BLM’s fresh map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

    Sources indicate that gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

    “Trails are kind of living things,” Ray remarked. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

    Move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

    Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray stated.

    “If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she said. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

    For trail users like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she claims, it never will.

    “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett notes. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

    She added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

    In a recent development, “Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett remarked. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

    10 Editor-Approved Stocking Stuffers for Backpackers and Hikers

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • (Photo: Courtesy REI, Amazon, Minus 33 and Backcountry).
    • There’s nothing more delightful than rummaging around in an oversized sock to find a piece of backpacking gear you never knew you needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    (Photo: Courtesy REI, Amazon, Minus 33 and Backcountry).

    Smartwool Active Fleece Wind Headband.

    Black Diamond Astro 300-R Headlamp.

    There’s nothing more delightful than rummaging around in an oversized sock to find a piece of backpacking gear you never knew you needed. Even if your giftee isn’t overwhelmed with joy (we’re sure they will be), these micro-gifts won’t set you back like an expensive, ill-fitting sleeping bag might. From energy chews to our current favorite pocket knife, here are ten backpacker-tested stocking stuffers, all small enough to fit into a hipbelt pocket.

    Hydration and electrolytes are a stacked category, but we love that Tailwind uses easy-to-drink, naturally-flavored mixes instead of unpronounceable ingredients. The 25-serving bulk bag is a good economical choice, but if single-serving packets are more convenient, you can opt for a variety pack instead. For super sweaty hikers, Saltt drink mixes add a dose of sodium to the blend without making it taste like seawater.

    Hiking hard in the heat can be a recipe for an upset stomach, but hikers still have to eat enough to power their miles. Skratch’s energy chews are some of the easiest to get down thanks to the varied texture of the sour sugar coating and punchy flavors. Choose between caffeinated and non-caffeinated varieties, all with easy-to-digest carbs for a quick boost of energy that doesn’t entail gnawing on a dense protein bar.

    A headband might not seem like a thrilling gift, but no one is ever sad they threw it into their pack. Smartwool’s version is warm and wicking, blocking brisk winds around the forehead with a windproof panel and extra width around the ears for coverage. This is the perfect accessory for chilly-but-not-frigid hikes where a beanie is overkill, but the wind is turning your forehead into an ice cube.

    Leatherman might be best known for its ranch-ready multitools, but it also has a lovely line of reliable, lightweight pocket knives. The Skeletool KB weighs just over one ounce, has a built-in bottle opener, and a tensioned belt clip for securing to a pocket or an interior flap on your pack. We’ve carried this for weeks at a time without seeing any dulling or corrosion. If you want to go big, you can also spring for a high-end Benchmade Bugout Knife, which weighs 1.85 ounces and has a range of customization options.

    Industry observers note that remember being a kid and groaning when you got socks for Christmas? Those days are long gone—we don’t know any hiker who isn’t thrilled to unwrap a fresh pair of wool socks. These trail-ready socks have a moderate amount of cushioning and structure for support without feeling compressive. Made with 75-percent merino, they also have excellent odor-resistance and softness while still holding their shape.

    HydraPak has made impressive strides in its line of ultralight, packable filters in the past few years. This filter-and-bottle combination uses their flagship soft flask with one of our favorite hollow-fiber filters. The flow rate stays strong and fast for longer than other similar styles, and the tough, seam-welded TPU bottle can withstand a whole lot of squeezing. The wide mouth makes it easy to fill, and hikers can either squeeze it into a larger bottle for drinking water or drink directly from the filter.

    Black Diamond nailed it with this headlamp. The Astro 300 offers an excellent combination of low weight (just 2.65 ounces), night-hiker-approved 300-lumen output, and a conveniently integrated rechargeable battery, all at a reasonable price. It’s highly waterproof and durable for long, rugged outings, and the single button is easy to press while wearing gloves. The only downside is that it doesn’t include a red light. If that’s an glitch, Nitecore’s UT27 MCT Pro 800 is more expensive, but weighs the same and comes with a red light option.

    It has been revealed that though it gets less press than rolled ankles and bad knees, skin chafing is the sneaky destroyer of many good days on the trail. Keep your hiker’s inner thighs safe with a stick of Squirrel’s Nut Butter, which has a trimmed-down formula limited to natural ingredients like coconut oil, cocoa butter, and Vitamin E oil. It glides on smoothly, and each application lasts several hours. Fast-packers and people in more humid environments might also appreciate Run Slick, which has a roll-on formula that is among the most sweat-resistant we’ve ever tested.

    Even the most weight-conscious backpacker will spare a few grams in the food bag for instant coffee. Alpine Start dissolves in a flash in hot water, and can even be shaken up without gritty residue in colder water for iced coffee vibes. The brand uses single-origin beans from farms in Colombia, and each packet is perfect for 8-10 ounces of water.

    Recent findings suggest that wired headphones might be a technological relic, but for backpackers, the trend never died. We love the convenience of having one less thing to charge on the trail, and this pair from Skullcandy has excellent sound quality for a reasonable price. They’re also durable: The cords on our pair have survived over a month of daily use on-trail without separating. If you’re looking to splurge, Bose recently updated its flagship wired earbuds, and the bump in price gets you better noise-canceling and a clear in-line microphone for ordering pizza to the trailhead.

    #147871. I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1354 w)

    I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.
    • That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.
    • Recent findings suggest that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge).

    “How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.

    That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

    Recent findings suggest that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

    I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

    According to recent reports, fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

    In a recent development, I was 52, the age when menopause, graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something big to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from the beach, I bought a hooded, five-millimeter wetsuit and booties, and started surfing several mornings a week, collecting phone numbers of women I met in the lineup and parking lot.

    After decades of giving everything I had to everyone around me—work colleagues, kids, husband, dogs, parents, sisters—surfing was just for me.

    Soon I had built a community of women surfers aged 25 to 75 to join me for dawn patrol sessions at our break north of San Francisco and surf trips to Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, San Diego, and Santa Cruz.

    Surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

    Seeking guidance on how to surf through surgery recovery and treatment, I posted a message on the Facebook “Women Who Surf” group of 39,000: “I just got diagnosed with breast cancer and am looking for other women surfers who surfed through chemo, and surfed after a double mastectomy.”.

    A hundred women weighed in with personal experience of cancer and surfing. Most hadn’t surfed during surgery recovery or chemotherapy due to doctors’ orders, infection risk, weak immune systems, limited mobility, fatigue, and weakness.

    But one woman told me to go for it: Melanie Ezell, a 42-year-old substantial wave surfer, based in Oahu, who surfed through ovarian cancer. She became my role model, inspiring me to paddle out as soon as I could.

    That long-awaited day came after being grounded on land for seven weeks following my double mastectomy. It was three days after my first chemotherapy infusion when my plastic surgeon declared my chest incisions adequately healed. I drove immediately to the beach, paddled out, and felt triumphant when I caught my first wave of the session.

    And I kept paddling out through the remaining 11 rounds of chemotherapy.

    Sources indicate that on days when the swell was massive and I was weak with fatigue, I’d claw through the impact zone after riding a wave, leaving my arms drained of power and lungs gasping for air. Once safely outside breaking waves, I’d rest on my board and let sets roll past until my breathing slowed. Still, being in the ocean felt like an antidote to the toxic drugs coursing through my veins. I loved watching the birds and seals, scanning the horizon for incoming sets, paddling into a rising wave, feeling its energy connect with my board.

    Sometimes those sessions lasted only an hour because of my reduced stamina. But they always left me feeling stoked and alive, adjectives easily lost when you spend Tuesday afternoons hooked up to an IV bag pumping the sledgehammer drug Taxol into a port in your chest.

    It has been revealed that after my last chemotherapy session, I started ten rounds of targeted immunotherapy infusions (which I just concluded this month) and began posting GoPro videos on Instagram and Facebook of me surfing bald to inspire other women. I wanted them to see what it looks like when breast cancer takes your breasts and hair, but not your identity.

    Women from around the world reached out to share their own stories: Ellen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old massage therapist and mom surfing through rectal cancer in the chilly waters at the Oregon-California border; 32-year-old Lottie Bakewell from Cornwall, England, surfing through breast cancer and the demands of caring for her one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter; Belen Kimble, a 48-year-old former professional longboarder, World Surf League commentator, surf performance coach, and single mom in Latest South Wales, Australia, surfing through breast cancer; and Caroline Wilhelm, a 55-year-old surfer and competitor from Los Angeles who took my cue to keep surfing through her breast cancer.

    Backed by growing research showing that physical activity during cancer treatment offsets chemotherapy side effects and improves recovery and resilience, my little cohort of surfing cancer patients proves the ocean is not just a sanctuary, but an active prescription for healing.

    In a recent development, but you don’t have to be a surfer to reap the benefits of physical activity during cancer. A upcoming study of 45,530 women published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in September 2026 confirmed what my surf sisters and I already knew: regular exercise gives women going through breast cancer the strength to bounce back more fully and reclaim our lives after treatment. The study followed women for 15 years with data from the Women’s Health Initiative and found that keeping up physical activity and healthy habits prior to a cancer diagnosis acts as a powerful buffer against the physical toll of cancer treatments.

    The trick is to start with small amounts of exercise and work with your care team on a game plan to get active.

    It has been revealed that “Even if you are not an exerciser, you can still start an exercise regimen during chemotherapy,” noted my oncologist Eva Thomas, MD, from Kaiser Permanente Oakland in California, who encouraged and cheered on my surfing during chemotherapy. “It sounds counter-intuitive, but women tell me that when they push themselves to exercise, they feel better. Mood is better, sleep is better, energy is increased, and body aches are reduced.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2022, the American Society of Clinical Oncology released the first-ever exercise guidelines based on more than 100 clinical trials examining the link between exercise and cancer treatment. For anyone going through cancer who wants to get active, the American College of Sports Medicine created a step-by-step guide in 2024 with research benefits and resources. It outlines a path to get started.

    My own path began years before cancer, as a young woman fixated on surfing, who waited decades to act upon her dream.

    According to recent reports, looking back, I see that my surfing community—and the strength and identity it gave me—helped me to charge forward through the scariest chapter of my life. The takeaway lesson is useful for all women and men facing challenges: Don’t delay trying something new and scary. It may end up transforming, and saving, you.

    It has been revealed that danielle Cass lives with her husband in Northern California, where they raised their 26-year-old son, 23-year-old daughter, and dogs. When she’s not surfing with friends, she leads Responsible AI enablement at Microsoft. A two-minute short film about her midlife entry into surfing Learning to Surf at 52 screened at the 2022 San Diego Surf Festival. Follow her surfing through cancer adventures on Instagram @danielle.cass and Substack Danielle Rides the Cancer Wave.

    #147870. Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (937 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Remembering Chris Falkenstein, Long-time Yosemite Climber and Photographer

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors.
    • Sources indicate that chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer.
    • In a recent development, I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chris Falkenstein (left) and Don Reid (right) were long-time climbing partners and guidebook co-authors. (Photo: Courtesy Falkenstein Family Collection).

    Sources indicate that chris Falkenstein passed away peacefully on August 9, 2026 after a brave and exhaustive battle with cancer. Better known by many as Falky, Finkelstein, Steiny, Schwackenstein, or Commando, Chris wore many hats throughout his life: devoted husband and father, loyal friend, accomplished climber, photographer, skier, whitewater kayaker, windsurfer, mountain biker, self-proclaimed computer nerd, and passionate lover of Yosemite and the outdoors.

    In a recent development, I grew up climbing with my Dad, but it was always his sport. I enjoyed it, but pursued other sports. In a way, I don’t think I’ve found a climbing partner that was ever as dialed as he was. My Dad was so quiet and humble about his achievements; there were so many things he never mentioned. I remember being out climbing with him, when he would tell some story like, “We were out here in the ‘80s, blasting a boom box and climbing.” It turns out, he would be talking about a first ascent.

    Recent findings suggest that those who knew him will remember his adventurous spirit, his enthusiasm for life, and the joy he found in exploring the world around him. His love for the outdoors was infectious. And the memories he created along the way will live on in those fortunate enough to have shared in his adventures.

    When Chris arrived in Yosemite in 1972, he brought a foundation of climbing experience from the Gunks of New York. His natural athleticism, determination, and enthusiasm rapidly drew him into the dynamic and evolving climbing scene of Yosemite Valley. What began as an introduction to the Yosemite climbing community grew into a lifelong passion and a lasting legacy.

    He once remarked, “So off I went at 18 to explore climbing in Yosemite. Best decision of my life, and a true highlight… I consider my life beginning after 18. Stay young at heart forever if you can.”.

    Recent findings suggest that chris spent the remainder of his life in and around Yosemite, calling many places home over the years, including Camp 4, the Annex, Badger Pass, Sonora, Tuolumne Meadows, and El Portal. Eventually, he settled in Foresta, where he and his wife, Doe, retired to the home they built together.

    Industry observers note that throughout his years in Yosemite, Chris became a respected presence in the climbing community, known for being a quiet and humble force. He established multiple first ascents in Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows. Among his notable first ascents were Do or Fly (5.11c), The Speed of Life (5.11b), Black Angel (5.11a), and Highway Star (5.10a). Along with Don Reid, he co-authored Rock Climbs of Tuolumne Meadows, first published in 1983. Four additional editions later followed. He also authored Yosemite Sport Climbs in 1992. Through his climbs, guidebooks, and contributions to the community, Chris helped shape and document Yosemite’s rich climbing history.

    According to recent reports, beyond his physical accomplishments in climbing, he inspired others and expanded the appreciation for the outdoors through his photography, videography, and online content. He captured the many aspects of climbing, mountaineering, and skiing, while sharing the extraordinary beauty of Yosemite.

    Chris’s work appeared in a wide range of publications, climbing guides, gear catalogs, climbing films, commercials, Hollywood productions, and websites. Chris’s photography became a familiar part of the Yosemite landscape itself. As Don Reid once remarked with a teasing smirk, “You know you are made with Yosemite photography when your photos appear on the Coke machines, shuttle buses, and climbing guide covers of the place.”.

    When it was too cold to climb, Chris also had a deep love for winter sports. He played hockey throughout his life and contributed to the local pick up hockey club in Yosemite. Alongside Bruce Brossman and Loyd Price, Chris completed the first single-day trans-Sierra ski trip via Tioga Pass. His name also lives on through several first descents in the Sierras, including the Solstice Couloir and Powerhouse Chute.

    At Badger Pass Ski Resort, Chris spent many years serving as ski patrol manager. He brought his knowledge of climbing techniques into ski patrol training, developing methods for chairlift rescues and assisting with backcountry rescue efforts. His impact was perhaps best captured by a skier he helped, who later described him as “an angel emerging from the woods.”.

    According to recent reports, early in his career, Chris worked for the Yosemite Climbing School, teaching climbing during the summer months and cross-country skiing in winter. He enjoyed summers as the employee housing manager in Tuolumne Meadows. In retirement, Chris continued to explore and enjoy the Sierras, while taking great pride in perfecting the art of being a grandfather. Chris also became an unofficial voice of Yosemite locals, keeping friends and former park residents connected to the place they loved by sharing updates and insights into the ever-changing landscape of Yosemite.

    Chris loved everything Yosemite. He devoted much of his time to documenting not only the climbing, skiing, and athletic pursuits that made the park famous, but also its immense beauty, extensive history, and the development and change over time. With an eye for the extraordinary as well as the everyday, he captured the moments, places, and details that might otherwise go unnoticed. Through his lens and storytelling, Chris shared his deep appreciation for Yosemite. In so doing, he preserved a piece of its story for others.

    Chris is survived by his wife Doe, his son Alex, his daughter-in-law Danielle, and his two-and-a-half-year-old grandson Finn, who loves trying to climb up anything in his path.

    #147867. A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1138 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    A Very Serious Story About Falling Asleep While Belaying

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans.
    • It has been revealed that significant falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope.
    • This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The East Face of Mount Temple, Canada, and the scene of this story's shenanigans. (Photo: Mitra Samavaki / Getty).

    It has been revealed that significant falls are commonplace while sport climbing and bouldering, but, in my opinion, the high alpine remains largely a safe space to take your brake hand off the rope. Why? With loose rock, aerated ice, and an often minimalist rack, falling off—even with a tight belay—usually spells disaster. A climber has every reason to follow the old “the leader cannot fall” ethos.

    This old school state of mind deeply resonated with me earlier this month on a difficult alpine climb on Mount Temple in the Canadian Rockies. This 1,400-meter ice and mixed route began easily enough, with a hike up a hard-packed snow slope at 6 a.m. toward the deep cleft that marked the start. Neither my partner Rory nor I were burdened with rope management during the first hour of climbing, since our rope stayed neatly coiled in a pack.

    Sources indicate that hundreds of meters higher, below one of the crux pitches, we flaked out our rope. Above us stood a terribly skinny pillar of ice no wider than my shoulders at its base. Blue light filtered through its entirety, a sign of its youth and untrustworthiness.

    “I don’t think I should place a screw in that,” Rory decided.

    I scanned the shattered quartzite behind the pillar, hoping to at least keep us attached to the mountain before Rory essentially soloed the pitch. Two nervous pitons and a shallow micro nut were all I could cobble together after 10 minutes of searching. I stomped out a waist-deep hole in the snow on the back side of the pillar and clipped into our wobbly anchor. My now four-piece anchor—plus Rory’s unshakeable climbing ability—gave us great odds of surviving his lead.

    The runout pitch gave me ample opportunity to pay out slack as I pleased while munching on trail mix and rehydrating from our busy morning. After all, Rory was not allowed to fall, so he didn’t.

    In a recent development, falling has been a frowned-upon practice for most of climbing’s history, especially before sport climbing became popular in the 1980s. Only relatively recently, and only in some styles of climbing, have leader falls become no longer taboo—even acceptable and encouraged.

    The crusty old-timer in me knows that, in any form of free climbing, it is always safer to climb to the top of a pitch without testing your equipment, be it a skinny rope, crashpad, or ice screw. This gut instinct evolved from a time when climbing gear was not completely trustworthy. Maybe you hand-stitched your quickdraw’s webbing yourself. Maybe you’d sourced your climbing protection from a hardware store. Or maybe you had tied your lead line around your waist because drop-seat harnesses hadn’t been invented yet. In this era—really only a few decades ago—your climbing ability was the first line of defense. Ropes and harnesses and removable protection served merely as dubious back-ups.

    But the advent of regular whippers is a tragedy for one more reason: With newfangled belay devices, hang dogging, and constant pleas to “watch me,” belaying has become a real pain in the ass.

    Industry observers note that nearly 12 hours later, Rory and I were still on Mount Temple. We’d topped out the ice climbing portion of the face and traversed across open snow slopes and through rock bands to a final serrated crux: the Black Towers. Countless turrets of dark limestone slice across the summit ridge of Mount Temple, creating difficult route finding even on a clear summer’s day. We were approaching midnight in November and a thick fog had choked the upper mountain. Visibility hovered around 10 meters. I had no idea where we were supposed to go.

    Thankfully it was Rory’s lead again, and he was questing. Fifteen minutes ticked by as he wandered up a steep rocky groove, then another 15 of the rope unmoving. An hour passed. I clicked off my headlamp to save battery. More time passed. I figured I could tie off the rope and catch a few Zs, so I did. Sleep felt amazing. I was glad that even as we approached 24 hours on the move, Rory still knew the rules: The leader cannot fall. And the belayer gets to sleep.

    I woke up to the sound of Rory’s voice. He’d been blocked by an overhang and was downclimbing. Thick, icy fog obscured our vision as I took the rack and traversed along a snow ledge looking for easier passage. The fog would sometimes lift for an instant—I’d spot a lonely star above—and I’d frantically flick my headlamp to full strength to catch a glimpse of the mountain. But before my eyes could adjust to the latest sight, the fog would crash back in like a breaking wave, drowning us in uncertainty once again.

    Recent findings suggest that this story does not end in a climbing success. We did not ultimately find our way through the Black Towers, nor did we share a weary, satisfied hug on the summit of Mount Temple. We became lost and a little delirious on a large mountain in the middle of the night and needed to go down.

    It has been revealed that we stayed roped together as we retraced our steps through deep snow on the upper mountain. I was a little worried about triggering an avalanche, but mainly I was just exhausted. If I stumbled, I would prefer to slide 30 meters before being caught by the rope than well over a thousand into the next life.

    It has been revealed that rory and I regrouped at an anchor I’d built in an outcrop of yellow rock. He led out across another snowfield which terminated at a gigantic notch in an otherwise sheer ridgeline. The notch marked the start of a classic ski descent, the 60-degree Aemmer Couloir, and our escape hatch. Rory trudged toward it and I paid out rope, nodding off again.

    Suddenly, I was awake. I had not pooped all day, yet the kilogram of trail mix and sausage and cheese I’d downed was making a basement appearance.

    It has been revealed that “Rory! Do you need a real belay for this bit? I really need to poo,” I yelled into the fog.

    “No, I don’t care,” the fog yelled back.

    I let the rope feed through the anchor, then unclipped it from my belay device and, without moving even a step away from our anchor, unloaded into the snow bank.

    According to recent reports, it would have been a disgusting mess had Rory fallen and weighted the anchor, dragging me into my own steaming waste. But he didn’t, and I made it back to civilization with both my dignity and my life intact.

    #147865. The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

    The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year.
    • It has been revealed that now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls at the moment under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA).
    • In November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year. The granite obelisk once stood in the open Chihuahuan Desert, in a remote area visited by few except hikers either starting or ending their journeys. The dirt road approaching it, Commodore Road, was unmaintained and required high-clearance vehicles, limiting access and traffic.

    It has been revealed that now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls at the moment under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA). Government contractors graded and widened the road from 8 feet to 24 feet to accommodate construction vehicles. For now, hikers can still enter the NDA with permission and touch the monument—whether they’re starting northbound or ending their CDT hike. However, security guards will eventually usher them away, out of the construction zone.

    In November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus. Neither had been there since construction began in early 2026.

    In a recent development, “We wanted to see on the ground what was actually happening and what people were experiencing,” Martinez told Backpacker. She described the scene as “surreal.”.

    Arriving at the terminus monument, Martinez and Labert watched as two hikers approached in the distance. The two women, trail names Geisha Girl and Fearless, marched toward them, border walls standing on both sides. In an emotional moment, the teary-eyed hikers walked right up to the monument.

    It has been revealed that “I think if they hadn’t been able to put their hands on the physical monument, even though it was between the two barriers, it would have been devastating,” Martinez said. “The importance of having access to that now while it’s under construction is so fundamental.”.

    Recent findings suggest that while these changes are striking to someone like Martinez, who has visited this terminus hundreds of times during her work with the non-profit trail organization, she says she sees a silver lining. The construction traffic is annoying, loud, disruptive, and changes the experience of finishing or starting your CDT hike in a quiet corner of the desert. But the improvements to Commodore Road greatly increase access to the trail’s southern terminus.

    Recent findings suggest that “Building a road invites more people, which means more people can get there, which is a beautiful thing. They can drive their loved ones to the trail and pick them up from the trail much easier than it ever has been,” she said. But at the same time, the improvements make it feel less remote, and could make it significantly busier. “So it’s bittersweet,” she said.

    In a recent development, sometime “in the near future,” Martinez remarked the terminus monument will be moved out of the NDA. Then, the CDTC will create a upcoming one with accurate longitude and latitude markers. She sees that as an opportunity to rethink how the monument will be dedicated and to include indigenous voices that weren’t involved when the original monument was dedicated in 1974.

    Asked what hikers should expect when approaching the southern terminus of the CDT, Martinez paused thoughtfully.

    Industry observers note that “I think they should be prepared for an amazing experience in one of the most beautiful places on the planet,” she said. “But you’re going to see this infrastructure now that didn’t exist before. And I would ask people to lean into the good stuff and then also use that moment as an opportunity to reflect on how the experience is making them feel.”.

    #147864. Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Put Your Rock Shoes in the Oven—You’ll Thank Us

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home.
    • I learned my first curse words on a chalky, sweat-stained gym mat.
    • Recent findings suggest that if there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A pinhole image of a person peering into their oven at home. (Photo: Getty Images).

    I grew up in a gym. I learned my first curse words on a chalky, sweat-stained gym mat. I got my first tattoo with the friends I did four-by-fours with. First boyfriend, even.

    Recent findings suggest that if there’s one thing that has held true over my years of cramming my feet into tiny, downturned rock shoes for the sake of performance, it’s that breaking in shoes sucks. Every time, no getting around it, a horrible experience. During one gym session, a friend said she’d pay to have someone break in her shoes for her. We were the same size, and I was pretty desperate for money at the time—but still, some things just aren’t worth it. And when you not only have to break in the shoes, but have a double training session ahead of you while your feet are screaming with pain? I’m sure that I cried once over it.

    When the pandemic hit, suddenly I wasn’t going to the gym anymore. And because—at least at the beginning—nobody was sure about transmission via holds outside, I refrained from climbing rock as well. During that turbulent time, a funny thing happened: Either my feet flattened out or my tolerance for tiny shoes decreased. Because when gyms reopened and I tried to push myself through the break-in process again, suddenly it felt a lot more hateful.

    As I complained loudly (and probably all while looking desperate) at Monkey House Carbondale in December 2020, a local friend, the pro climber Dan Mirsky, overheard me.

    “Try putting ‘em in the oven,” he stated.

    Recent findings suggest that “No way. They’ll delaminate!” I protested.

    It has been revealed that “No, seriously. Just for a few minutes on the lowest setting. Game-changer.”.

    I took his tip, which I later learned he had originally gotten from another pro climber, Jonathan Siegrist, to heart. That night, I set up my station: oven, on the lowest setting (170 degrees), timer, and area on the carpet where I would dance around like a circus monkey. In the shoes went, for two minutes. I would then wear them for five to ten minutes—pacing, with some good ol’ fashioned calf raises mixed in—and then they’d go back in the oven, for another cycle or two. (Note: This only works with a standard oven, not a microwave—do not microwave your rock shoes or it will severely damage/deform them!).

    I couldn’t believe the results. Those brand-newly introduced puppies felt more akin to the pair you sweated in all summer and have yet to send to a resoler (God bless the person who has to touch that pair). It was one of those moments when you realize your life has changed forever.

    Sources indicate that and a fun fact for you, which I learned with more research: Leather stretches when wet (duh!). So try the oven thing, plus adding a sprinkling of water when they shoes are still hot, prior to donning them. And voilà! Your warm, wet shoes will slide right on and stretch even more.

    According to recent reports, curious for his take, I reached out to Siegrist. “Yes, I do that sometimes!” he wrote. “Not as much any more, because I think I just simply get bigger shoes. Ha!”.

    And that, actually, might just be the best tip of all.

    Note: While the author has successfully applied this tip on multiple occasions, as has Siegrist and Mirsky, not all shoemakers recommend. Scarpa, for example, has noted that this method of breaking in shoes will reduce glue strength and void shoe warranty.

    #147863. Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (476 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (476 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outsideonline

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).
    • A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.
    • On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).

    A fresh law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

    On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

    If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

    In a recent development, the decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate organization. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

    Industry observers note that lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk was almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself, lawmakers stated.

    “Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” Padilla noted in a statement. “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that jackie McGuinness, Padilla’s communications director, told Outside that the agreement will change Yosemite’s boundaries. A map McGuinness sent shows the park boundaries shifting to the east, filling in a checkerboard pattern left blocked out by the previous perimeter lines.

    USFS manages land ranchers use for livestock grazing on national forests and grasslands, while the NPS restricts most of these operations within park boundaries. The land exchange between the two agencies eliminates confusion caused by the jurisdictional split, McClintock said in a U.S. House floor statement on September 14.

    According to recent reports, “The proposed land exchange would make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction,” he noted. “Ranchers need to know where their permits apply, where infrastructure can be maintained, and who is responsible for decisions affecting their operations.”.

    It’s unclear whether or when Trump intends to sign the bill into law.

    The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In
